metadata.title: The Alert Nobody Hardcoded
metadata.purpose: Provenance Gatekeeper Development Log, Week 9 — wiring the Gatekeeper to an n8n incident pipeline: Docker-networked services, a visual severity router, a fired adversarial payload, and what one green execution does and does not prove.

metadata.series_note: Week 4 (Silent Failures) already covered SQLite incident logging and a raw outbound webhook. This reel deliberately foregrounds only what is NEW in Week 9 — Docker-networked service-to-service delivery, a visual canvas with severity routing, and decoupling from vendor SDKs — and is titled distinctly so the two do not collide in the playlist.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Onkar Bhujbal. The Provenance Gatekeeper is doing its job — intercepting hallucinated numbers and blocking them before they reach production. But a blocked error written to a local SQLite file is a secret. If a critical financial discrepancy fires at two in the morning, nobody is reading that table. This week I connected the service to an automated incident pipeline.

Detecting it is half.
Logging is the other half.

beats.narration_text: So that the local environment mirrors the eventual cloud deployment, I orchestrated both the FastAPI Gatekeeper and the n8n automation engine with Docker Compose. The naive version publishes the automation platform's port to the host, which means to the internet. Instead, both services sit on the same internal Docker network. The Gatekeeper reaches n8n by service name — and nothing outside the compose file can reach it at all.
beats.new_visual_element: The port that should not be published

show.event: left panel lands: the naive compose fragment
on 'to the internet', the published port highlights terracotta IN PLACE
note lands beneath: anyone who finds the host can POST to the workflow
right panel reveals the internal-network version
ink stamp lands: NO PUBLIC PORT

props.sparkLine: Same host. Two very different doors.
props.hotNote: published to the host — and to anything that can reach the host
props.code:
services:
  gatekeeper:
    networks: [backplane]
  n8n:
    networks: [backplane]
    # no ports: published

networks:
  backplane:
    internal: true

# POST http://n8n:5678/webhook/...
props.stampSub: service-to-service by name; nothing outside the compose file can reach it

beats.honesty_note: The compose fragments are minimal and illustrative — the real file carries images, volumes and env. The security point is exact: a published port is reachable by anything that can reach the host, and `internal: true` removes that route.

beats.narration_text: Rather than hardcoding a chat vendor's S.D.K. into the Python service — which is technical debt the moment anyone changes tools — the service exports one incident payload and stops caring. On the n8n canvas, three nodes do the rest: catch the webhook, read the JSON body, route on severity. A magnitude error takes the high-priority branch and is formatted for the on-call channel.

beats.narration_text: To test it end to end I fired the automated adversarial payload at the secure endpoint — a false four-point-five-million-dollar claim. The Gatekeeper rejected it, generated the error explanation, wrote the row, and fired the webhook. Seconds later the same incident appeared in the n8n execution log, timestamps matching. The write and the shout now happen together.

beats.narration_text: The script I wrote for this said the pipeline works flawlessly. It does not — one successful execution proves the happy path and nothing else. The Gatekeeper fires and forgets. If the n8n container is restarting, that POST fails into a log line nobody reads, which is exactly the problem I started the week trying to solve. Until there is a retry, a dead-letter queue, and an alert that fires when alerting itself fails, what I have is a pipeline that worked once.

beats.authoring_note: BEAT ADDED. The supplied script's Scene 4 claims the pipeline 'works flawlessly'; one execution cannot support that. The honest failure is recursive and worth the beat: an undelivered alert degrades to exactly the silent log row the reel opened on.

beats.narration_text: So: don't clutter a microservice with third-party messaging libraries. Emit one neutral incident payload, route it outside the code — and treat the delivery itself as something that can fail.

show.event: code card opens on a hard cut; traffic-light dot arms terracotta
the emitter reveals — one POST, no vendor import
the TASK line lands: decouple your alert logic
the last note lands — the delivery failure is itself an incident

props.title: alerts.py
props.code:
def emit(incident: dict) -> None:
    # no slack_sdk. no smtplib. no vendor.
    r = post("http://n8n:5678/webhook/incident",
             json=incident, timeout=3)
    if not r.ok:
        dead_letter(incident)   # try again later
        page_oncall("alerting is down")

# TASK: decouple your alert logic.

beats.authoring_note: The dead_letter and page_oncall lines are the reel's addition — they are what turns the Week 9 integration from a demo into a pipeline.

beats.narration_text: Here is the prompt worth running against your own alerting. Ask a model what happens when the notification service is the thing that is down. If the answer is a log line, you have the same problem I did — you just haven't had the outage yet.
